title: Request, Response, and Router Abstractions
learning_outcomes: Explain what request, response, and router abstractions contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: request objects.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. In this lesson, focus on request objects; then compare it with response objects. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use request, response, and router abstractions when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. For request, response, and router abstractions, begin with request objects. Also distinguish response objects; route definitions; middleware concepts. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Request, Response, and Router Abstractions
content_blocks.code:
<?php
interface Notifier { public function send(string $message): string; }
final class LogNotifier implements Notifier { public function send(string $message): string { return "logged: " . $message; } }
echo (new LogNotifier())->send("ready") . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
